An approval loop that resolves the approver's Discord id to a name, substitutes it into the signature, re-reads the live thread, writes the ledger before any send could fire, and prints the final message. 56 adversarial variants, 0 disagreements. Blueprint in the vault at 30 - Resources/Bot Blueprints/echo-bot.md; the price rule is its own skill.
detail.needsImprovement: Echo can only answer half the weekend, and the limit is missing inputs rather than writing quality. Of 27 actionable leads: 6 asked about a price nobody had quoted them, 4 asked for PPF which the shop does not do, 3 needed scheduling. The parked Quote Unblocker feeds the first group and the existing capacity report covers the third, and either does more for coverage than any prose improvement. Missed calls remain out of scope and are the bigger cohort. There is no expiry mechanism, no circuit breaker and no ledger-enforced idempotency on send, because nothing can send — all three have to be built with the send path, not after it.
detail.watchFor:
Noise and double-texting, unchanged and still how this fails.

Never let anything compute a price. Three numbers on one proposal all look correct and only invoice.total is what the customer was quoted; the discount label itself is off by three points on at least one live proposal. Any change that sums, subtracts or applies a percentage reintroduces an $825 error. And a right price for the wrong car is still a wrong price — a Corvette question against a Model Y proposal produced the Model Y's number.

Do-not-contact is per channel. Of six weekend opt-outs, all six were blocked on text and five had email, calls and WhatsApp open, so a cross-channel reply would have reached someone who wrote STOP. Replying only on the channel they used is what makes that safe, so it is a guard and not a preference.

Read what the customer typed, not what is in the thread. Our own marketing arrives labelled inbound and byte-identical to what we sent. iPhone tapbacks arrive as inbound and are our own words quoted back. Inbound email arrives with no body at all. And most inbound email is a reply to a nurture send with our whole newsletter quoted underneath, asking about something unrelated — that shape was discarding real questions until 9/02.

A similarity score cannot gate a draft. 'Customer wants to rent a car' — never offered, never answered — scores 75% on the reranker, one point below a genuine reschedule. Whether the retrieved exemplar is the same KIND of message is checkable; how similar it is, is not.

Instagram closes after 7 days, and a draft approved after the window shuts is rejected outright. This has already happened once, approved nine hours late.

On Discord specifically: server permissions are not enough, a channel-level override kept every channel unreadable until the bot was added to the channel's own permission list, and the failure is a silent 403 with no error anywhere.

sessions.title: Built the reference book for how GoHighLevel actually works under the hood: seven endpoints documented, and the official docs caught out on eleven counts
shipped: Started a reusable reference folder, ghl-api-assets/, for how GoHighLevel actually works under the hood, and wrote the first entry: how the system fetches the written record of a phone call. Opened a real 12-minute call in GoHighLevel with the network recorder running, cleared it, clicked View Transcript once, and caught the exact request the software sends. One click, never repeated, nothing sent or changed. The entry carries the request, a ready-to-run example, and an example of what comes back, with every customer name, phone number, email, ID, and word of real conversation stripped out.

Confirmed the request goes to GoHighLevel's official public address, not a private back-door one, which means we can build on it without it disappearing in an update. It does carry one undocumented extra setting the web app adds, and that is flagged as the single open risk worth testing, because if it turns out to be a page marker we could be reading only the first slice of a long call and never know.

Checked the write-up against 9,750 real transcript lines already saved on this machine, from 210 calls across 80 files, rather than trusting the official documentation. That is what turned up the four errors below.

Extended the reference folder from one entry to seven, covering the pieces every automation we run depends on: reading a contact, reading a conversation, the written record of a call, the call audio, moving a deal to another stage, adding someone to an automated sequence, and booking an appointment. Each entry says what we watched happen, what we measured from real saved data, what we read in our own code, and what is only HighLevel's word for it, so nobody has to guess which parts are trustworthy.

Marked three of the seven as NOT verified, on purpose. Moving a deal, enrolling someone in a sequence, and booking an appointment all change real things, so I documented them without firing them. The ready-to-run examples for those three refuse to do anything unless you explicitly switch them on, and I tested that they refuse. The other four are read-only and just fetch information.
Measured the real answers instead of trusting the manual: 491 saved contact records, 20,328 saved messages, 210 call transcripts, and 5,899 deal records. That is what turned up the errors below.
fixed: The official documentation describes the wrong answer shape. It says one block comes back; what actually comes back is a list. Code written to the documentation gets nothing and shows no error. That exact bug already cost us every transcript on 235 calls once before.
Timestamps are in seconds, not the thousandths of a second the documentation states. Anyone trusting the documentation would place every quoted moment in a call 1,000 times too far along.
A call with no transcript comes back as an error, not as an empty result. If we treat that as a failure, one untranscribed call kills the whole batch and we lose the rest of the day's calls with it.

Speaker labelling is missing entirely on 115 of the 210 calls checked, so we cannot promise to tell the customer's words from ours on roughly half of them. The documentation implies it is always there. Anything we build that separates who said what has to cope with it being absent.

Reading a contact hides anything that is switched off. If a customer has not asked us to stop contacting them, that fact is simply missing from the record rather than marked false. Code that checks whether the field is there decides everyone is off-limits: on September 7 that parked 1,382 of 1,390 people. The fix is in the write-up, with the safe way to check consent in bulk.
Our own system logs a phone call with no message text at all, not blank text. Any code that reads it the ordinary way crashes or silently skips every call.

Call length is recorded as unknown on 82 of 337 calls, and 39 of those are calls that actually connected and were completed. The common shorthand for handling that quietly rewrites all 39 as nobody-answered, so we would never fetch what was said on 39 real sales conversations.

Writing down what one click of Add to workflow really costs: it hands a customer to a live sequence that sends six branded emails over eight days from Noah's address, the last one asking whether to close their file. Removing them afterwards stops future emails but cannot unsend the ones already gone. That is now the first thing anyone reads on that page, not a footnote.

Booking an appointment through the API has a setting that skips the is-this-slot-free check and another that silently ignores a repeat booking while still reporting success. Both are flagged, along with the fact that notifications to the customer are ON unless you turn them off.
inProgress: Three of the seven cannot be finished without a decision. Verifying them means moving a real deal on the board, sending a real customer six real emails, or putting a real booking on the calendar. They stay documented-but-unverified until Tasha says which, if any, is worth doing and on whom.

Two cheap read-only checks would close most of the remaining gaps: one to confirm whether our key can touch calendars at all (we think it cannot), and one comparing a long call's transcript with and without an undocumented setting, to rule out that we have been reading only the first slice.
sessions.notes: Nothing here needs Noah. The point of the folder is that the next person, or the next version of me, does not re-derive this from scratch or trust documentation that is wrong in eleven places. Every claim is tagged with where it came from: watched live, measured from saved data, read from our own code, or taken from HighLevel's documentation and not verified.
